blocks.text: Some resource families are far too large, or too open ended, to ever list out one by one. A file system might hold millions of files, a database table millions of rows, and no server should have to enumerate every single one just so a client can ask for it.
Resource templates solve this by handing the client a pattern instead of a list, a parameterized URI shape it can fill in itself to construct a valid resource URI for any member of that family.
This lesson looks at what a template is, how a server declares one, and how a client actually uses it.
1. What a Resource Template Is
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252136-710626285.png

A resource template is a URI pattern with one or more placeholder segments that a client fills in to produce a concrete, valid resource URI. Instead of a server listing every file in a project one by one, it can advertise a single template, file:///{path}, and let a client construct file:///project/src/app.py itself whenever it needs that specific file, without the server ever having had to enumerate it in advance.

This is a genuinely different mechanism from both static and dynamic resources covered in the previous two lessons. Static and dynamic resources are both things a server hands a client through resources/list, complete and ready to read. A template is something a client uses to build a URI on its own, based on a pattern the server described rather than an item the server listed.

A helpful way to picture the difference is a phone book versus a formula. A static or dynamic resources/list is the phone book, every entry spelled out. A template is closer to a formula for looking someone up if you already know their name, no phone book required, as long as you supply the right input.
2. The Problem Templates Solve

Think about a server wrapping a database with a hundred million rows. Listing every row as an individual resource entry would be absurd, both far too slow to compute and far too large to return in any single response. Yet a client might still reasonably want to fetch one specific row by its primary key, if it already knows that key from context, a previous tool call, a user's question, or an earlier resource it read.

A resource template closes this gap perfectly. The server declares db://orders/{orderId} once, and a client that already knows an order id of 48213, from anywhere, a previous conversation turn, a search result, can construct db://orders/48213 immediately and read it directly, without the server ever needing to enumerate all hundred million rows.
3. URI Template Syntax
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252136-537743697.png

MCP resource templates use the same curly-brace placeholder syntax as RFC 6570 URI templates, a widely used standard for exactly this kind of parameterized URI. A placeholder is written as a name inside curly braces, and a client substitutes a real value for that name to produce a concrete URI.
Each {name} segment names exactly what the client needs to supply, and a well chosen name doubles as documentation, orderId is far clearer than the generic id.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: The placeholder name inside curly braces is not just cosmetic, some clients surface it directly to a user or a model when prompting for a value, so a clear, specific name genuinely improves the experience.

blocks.text: 4. Declaring a Resource Template

A server declares a template much like it declares a static resource, but through a dedicated templates listing rather than the ordinary resources array, since a template is not itself a directly readable resource, it is a pattern describing a whole family of them.
A template descriptor should also carry a mimeType when every resource that pattern resolves to shares one, sparing a client from having to guess the content type of something it has not fetched yet.
5. The resources/templates/list Method

A client discovers available templates through resources/templates/list, a sibling method to resources/list, returning an array of template descriptors rather than concrete resources. A client typically calls this once early in a session, alongside resources/list, to build a full picture of both the concrete resources a server already knows about and the patterns it can construct on demand.

It is worth noting that resourceTemplates and resources are two entirely separate arrays in a client's mental model of a server, even though both eventually produce URIs a client can pass to resources/read. Keeping this separation clear avoids the confusion of expecting a template to show up inside a plain resources/list response.
6. How a Client Fills In a Template

blocks.alt: How a Client Fills In a Template
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252136-374070452.png

Once a client has a template and a value for its placeholder, constructing the concrete URI is simple string substitution, replace {orderId} with the actual order id, and the result is a URI ready to pass to resources/read exactly as if it had come from a resources/list call.

code.content:
# Filling in a template, pseudocode
template = "db://orders/{orderId}"
order_id = "48213"
uri = template.replace("{orderId}", order_id)
# uri is now "db://orders/48213"

content = await session.read_resource(uri)

blocks.text: The tricky part is rarely the substitution itself, it is knowing what value to substitute. That value has to come from somewhere, a tool result, a previous resource, or something the user typed, since the client cannot invent a valid order id out of nowhere.
7. Multiple Parameters in One Template

A template can have more than one placeholder when a resource is identified by more than one piece of information, a wiki article identified by both a space and a slug, for instance. A client needs a value for every placeholder before it can construct a valid URI, partial substitution does not produce anything a server can resolve.

When a template has several placeholders, it is good practice to order them from broadest to narrowest, the way wiki://{space}/{slug} moves from a whole space down to one article, mirroring how a person would naturally narrow down what they are looking for.
8. Templates vs Enumerated Static Lists
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252136-758441458.png

It is worth being precise about when a template is the right tool versus a static list, covered two lessons ago. A static list is right when the full set is small and worth enumerating up front, four config files, a dozen documentation chapters. A template is right when the family is too large to enumerate, or genuinely open ended, any file under a project directory, any row in a growing table.

blocks.title: Worth remembering
blocks.content: A server is free to offer both at once, a small static list of frequently used resources plus a template covering the long tail nobody would want listed in full.

blocks.text: 9. Templates vs Dynamic Discovery
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252137-621663572.png

Templates and dynamic resources solve a related but distinct problem. Dynamic resources are still something the server enumerates, just freshly at call time, search results, currently open tickets. A template is never enumerated by the server at all, the client itself constructs the URI, meaning the server does not even need to know every possible value ahead of time, only how to resolve one once handed a filled-in URI.

blocks.text: A useful mental shortcut: if you find yourself wanting to call resources/list just to get a URI you could have constructed yourself from information already in hand, a template is very likely the better design, saving a full round trip purely to learn a shape you could predict.
10. Validating Constructed URIs

Because a client constructs the URI itself, a well behaved server needs to validate it on the read side just as carefully as it would validate any other input, checking that a substituted orderId is a real order, that a substituted path does not escape outside an intended directory, rather than trusting that anything shaped like the template is automatically safe.

items: Reject a substituted value that does not match the expected type or shape for that placeholder.
Never trust a substituted file path without normalizing and checking it stays within an intended root directory.
Return a clear, typed not-found error rather than an empty or default value when a substituted id does not exist.

blocks.text: 11. Templates for File Systems

File systems are the canonical example of a template-shaped resource family, file:///{path}, since a project can have an unbounded number of files and nobody wants a server enumerating every single one just to let a client fetch one file by its known path. A client that already knows a file's path, perhaps from a directory listing tool or from context in the conversation, constructs the URI directly.

A path placeholder in a file system template also needs the same care around special characters and encoding covered in the resource URIs lesson, since a raw, unencoded path segment could otherwise be misread or, worse, used to escape the intended directory entirely.
12. Templates for Databases

Database-backed servers are the other classic case, db://{table}/{id}, letting a client fetch one specific row once it has a primary key, without the server ever exposing the whole table as a resources/list response. This pairs naturally with a tool that performs a search or lookup and returns a set of ids, which the client then turns into resource URIs via the template to fetch full row content.

The same pattern extends naturally to nested resources, an order and its line items for instance, db://orders/{orderId}/items/{itemId}, letting a client drill down as far as it needs to with a single consistent scheme.
13. Templates for APIs and Web Resources

A server wrapping a third party API can expose a template mirroring that API's own addressing scheme, weather://{city}/forecast for a weather service, github://{owner}/{repo}/issues/{number} for a specific issue. This lets a client compose a URI directly from information it already has, without a separate lookup step just to discover what URIs exist.
14. When Not to Use a Template

blocks.alt: When Not to Use a Template
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252630-876059143.png

A template is the wrong tool when a client genuinely has no way to know a valid value for the placeholder without first asking the server, in which case a plain resources/list, static or dynamic, serves the client far better than a pattern it cannot fill in on its own. Offering a template for a family a client can never guess valid parameters for just shifts the burden of discovery back onto the client with no real benefit.

items: A client has no independent way to learn a valid order id, so a template alone leaves it stuck.
A small, fully enumerable set that would be simpler and clearer as a static list.
A family where nearly every constructed URI would be invalid, wasting round trips.

blocks.text: In every one of these cases, the underlying problem is the same: a template only helps when the client already possesses, or can easily obtain, a valid value for every placeholder. Whenever that condition does not hold, a plain enumerable list is simply the more honest design.
15. Documenting a Template for Humans and Models

Because a model acting through a client often has to decide, on its own, what value to substitute into a template, the description field on a template descriptor deserves real care, explaining plainly what kind of value each placeholder expects and where a reasonable value might come from.
16. Combining Templates with resources/list

Many real servers offer both a resources/list of a handful of frequently used or recently touched items, and a resourceTemplates/list covering the long tail, giving a client the best of both, a ready browsable set for common cases, and a flexible pattern for everything else. A client typically merges both results when presenting resources to a user or a model, so nothing feels artificially hidden.
17. RFC 6570 Compliance and Portability
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785440252630-612880932.png

Sticking to the plain curly-brace substitution style of RFC 6570, rather than reaching for its more exotic operators like prefix matching or reserved character expansion, keeps a template easy for both humans and client implementations to parse correctly. Most MCP clients only need to support this simple substitution form, so a server author gains little by using the standard's more advanced features and risks confusing a client that only implements the common subset.
18. Templates and Autocomplete

Some MCP clients build a lightweight autocomplete experience on top of a template, prompting a user for each placeholder value by name, using the template's description to explain what is expected. This turns a template from something only a model can use fluently into something a human typing directly into a client can use just as easily.
Worked Example

Consider an MCP server for a customer support platform. It exposes a small static list of the ten most recently updated tickets directly through resources/list, since those are the ones a support agent is likely to want immediately, and a template, ticket://support/{ticketId}, for fetching any ticket at all once its id is known.

An agent helping a support engineer can search for tickets by keyword through a tool, get back a handful of ticket ids, and then use the template to read the full content of exactly the ones relevant to the conversation, without the server ever needing to expose its entire ticket history as a resources/list response.
Common Mistakes

items: Offering a template for a family the client has no independent way to learn valid parameter values for.
Trusting a constructed URI without validating it on the read side, opening the door to path traversal or invalid lookups.
Writing vague placeholder names like {id} instead of specific ones like {orderId} that double as documentation.
Forgetting to expose resources/templates/list at all, leaving a client unaware a template-based path even exists.
Using a template where a small static list would have been simpler and clearer for both the client and whoever is reading the server's documentation.
Mixing up placeholder names between the template string and its description, confusing anyone trying to fill it in correctly.

blocks.text: Practice

Design a resource template for an MCP server that exposes invoices from a billing system, where each invoice has a unique numeric ID. Write the uriTemplate, a clear description, and one example of a client filling it in for invoice 9931.
Key Takeaway

A resource template is a parameterized URI pattern that lets a client construct a valid resource URI itself, covering an entire family of resources too large or open ended for a server to ever enumerate directly. It is discovered through resources/templates/list, filled in through simple substitution, and validated on the server side exactly as carefully as any other input.

The next lesson steps back to look at resource discovery as a whole, how a client finds out what a server offers in the first place, tying together resources/list, resources/templates/list, and a first look at pagination for when even a static or dynamic set grows too large for a single response.
